The experiments compare many closed- and open-source MLLMs and include per-dimension metrics, score-distribution analysis, and qualitative case studies.
The fine-tuning results are promising: VISJUDGE improves consistently over several open-source backbones and substantially outperforms general MLLMs on the proposed benchmark.
weaknesses: The central ground-truth validity is not fully convincing. Data fidelity is judged mostly from rendered images without source data, so the benchmark can detect visible distortions but cannot verify whether visualized values are actually accurate.

The paper repeatedly calls the dataset expert-annotated, but the main labels come from crowdsourced workers with expert review/adjudication. Inter-expert agreement and independent expert-only reliability are not reported.
The benchmark may contain web-crawling bias, source/style duplication, and train-test leakage risks; random stratified splitting is weaker than source-, domain-, or template-held-out evaluation.

External generalization evidence is limited. MatPlotAgent outputs are evaluated by GPT-4o, despite the paper arguing that MLLMs are unreliable visualization judges, which weakens the application claims.

Several claims are overstated, especially “first comprehensive benchmark,” “near-perfect alignment,” and deployment readiness. Statistical significance, confidence intervals, and robustness to prompt/model randomness are missing.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the abstract has an unfinished availability statement, and details about exact source filtering, released URLs/licenses, model outputs, and API inference conditions are not sufficient for a benchmark paper.

strengths: Addresses a real gap: evaluating visualization quality requires more than generic image aesthetics or chart QA, and the paper usefully separates fidelity, expressiveness, and aesthetics into concrete subdimensions.

The benchmark construction is reasonably broad in surface coverage, with 3,090 real-world visualizations spanning single charts, multi-view visualizations, and dashboards, plus multiple baselines including closed- and open-source MLLMs.

The empirical results are detailed and diagnostic: MAE/correlation tables, score-distribution analysis, complexity breakdowns, case studies, and downstream integrations give a useful initial picture of current MLLM failure modes.

Fine-tuning several open-source VLM backbones on the proposed labels consistently improves agreement with held-out benchmark annotations, suggesting that domain-specific supervision is valuable for visualization judging.
weaknesses: The central benchmark validity is not fully convincing. The paper claims to assess data fidelity, but most web-collected visualizations lack underlying raw data, so fidelity is judged only from visible surface cues. This conflates factual correctness with readability and makes the strongest claims about faithful data representation unsupported.

The annotation protocol lacks key reliability evidence. There are only three crowd labels per item, expert adjudication is described procedurally but without inter-expert agreement, calibration details, confidence intervals, or a clear statistical model for final labels. Treating expert-adjusted labels as gold standard is therefore underjustified.

The VISJUDGE evaluation is partly circular: the model is trained to imitate the benchmark labels and evaluated on a random held-out split from the same data collection and rubric-generation process. Stronger external validation with fresh human judgments or independently sourced datasets is needed.

The downstream application evidence is weak. MatPlotAgent improvements are evaluated automatically by GPT-4o rather than human experts, while GPT-4o is also used in dataset filtering/metadata/rubric generation, raising evaluator bias concerns. Reported recommendation gains are modest and lack significance testing.

Novelty is limited beyond dataset construction. The framework largely repackages known visualization quality criteria, and the model contribution is straightforward LoRA/GRPO fine-tuning on scalar rubric scores rather than a new method.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the abstract has a missing release URL, closed-source model versions/API dates are not specified, prompts and data release details are only partially described, and web-scraped image licensing/copyright handling is asserted but not demonstrated.

The dataset has notable coverage and bias issues: English/US-heavy annotators, web-search sampling bias, very sparse subtypes despite claims of 32 chart types, strong imbalance in dashboard quality, and limited support for interactive or dynamic visualizations.

Presentation and claims are sometimes overstated. Phrases such as “first comprehensive,” “near-perfect alignment,” and “human-like evaluation” exceed the evidence, and several figures/tables are cramped or difficult to read.
